For general advice about indexes, check out this [guide](https://github.com/orgs/supabase/discussions/22449). 13 14 ## **To speed up queries, it is ideal to create an HSNW index on your embedded column** 15 16 The general structure for creating an HNSW index follows this pattern: 17 18 ```sql 19 CREATE INDEX ON USING hnsw ( ); 20 ``` 21 22 Search can be one of three types: 23 operator | description | search type 24 -- | -- | -- 25 `<->` | Euclidean distance | vector_l2_ops 26 `<#>` | negative inner product | vector_ip_ops 27 `<=>` | cosine distance | vector_cosine_ops 28 29 Queries can only use the index if it matches the search type used. If you are unsure which search type to prioritize, vector_cosine_ops is the most commonly used. You can checkout our [guide](/docs/guides/ai/vector-indexes/hnsw-indexes) for more info. The folks at Crunchy Data also wrote an [explainer](https://www.crunchydata.com/blog/hnsw-indexes-with-postgres-and-pgvector) that you may find useful. 30 31 Applying an index can be slow and computationally expensive, so there are a few preparations that should be made beforehand: 32 33 **1. Make sure your pgvector is the latest available version on Supabase.** 34 35 Versions 0.6 and later have accelerated HNSW build speeds. You can observe your current version in the [Dashboard's Extensions Page](/dashboard/project/_/database/extensions). You can perform a software upgrade in the [General Settings](/dashboard/project/_/settings/general) if necessary. 36 37 **2. Setting up an external connection** 38 39 The Dashboard has an internal time limit of ~2 minutes for queries. Indexing a large table will almost always take more time, so it is necessary to execute your code through an external interface, such as PSQL. 40 41 You can install PSQL in [macOS](https://stackoverflow.com/a/49689589/2188186) and [Windows](https://www.postgresql.org/download/windows/) by following these links and instructions. 42 For Linux (Debian) you can run the following: 43 44 ```bash 45 sudo apt-get update 46 sudo apt-get install postgresql-client 47 ``` 48 49 Once installed, you can find your PSQL string on the dashboard by clicking [connect](/dashboard/project/_?showConnect=true). Make sure if you are using the pooler connection that it is the [Session pooler](/dashboard/project/_?showConnect=true&method=session) (port 5432). 50 51 If your network can use IPv6, consider using the direct connection string instead of Supavisor. It's not mandatory, but for tasks that run a long time, it's best to reduce network complexity. To check if your network is compatible, use this cURL command to request your IPv6 address: 52 53 ```bash 54 curl -6 https://ifconfig.co/ip 55 ``` 56 57 If an address is returned, you should use your direct connection string found on the dashboard by clicking [connect](/dashboard/project/_?showConnect=true). 58 59 **3. Increase memory for index creation (optional)** 60 61 The `maintenance_work_mem` variable limits the maximum amount of memory that can be used by maintenance operations, such as vacuuming, altering, and indexing tables. In your session you should try to set it to a reasonably high value: 62 63 ```sql 64 set maintenance_work_mem to ; -- '#GB' 65 ``` 66 67 Inspect value to make sure it has been set: 68 69 ```sql 70 show maintenance_work_mem; 71 ``` 72 73 **4. Increase cores for index creation (optional)** 74 75 The `max_parallel_maintenance_workers` variable limits the amount of cores that can be used by maintenance operations, including indexing tables. In your session, you should try to set it to a value roughly 1/2 to 2/3s of your [compute core amount](/docs/guides/platform/compute-and-disk): 76 77 ```sql 78 set max_parallel_maintenance_workers to ; 79 ``` 80 81 Inspect value to make sure it has been set: 82 83 ```sql 84 show max_parallel_maintenance_workers; 85 ``` 86 87 **5. Setting a custom timeout** 88 89 Disable query timeout for your connection: 90 91 ```sql 92 set statement_timeout = '0'; 93 ``` 94 95 Inspect value to make sure it has been set: 96 97 ```sql 98 show statement_timeout; 99 ``` 100 101 **6. Consider temporarily upgrading your compute size (optional)** 102 103 If your task is particularly long, you can speed it up by boosting your computing power temporarily. Compute size is charged by the hour, so you can increase it for an hour or two to finish your task faster, then scale it back afterwards. Here is a list of [compute add-ons](/docs/guides/platform/compute-and-disk). If you want to temporarily upgrade, you can find the add-ons for your project in your [Dashboard's Add-ons Settings.](https://supabase.green/dashboard/project/_/settings/addons) 104 105 **7. Consider increasing disk size (optional)** 106 107 HSNW indexes can produce temporary files during their construction that may consume a few GBs worth of disk. 108 Consider increasing the disk size in the [Infrastructure settings](/dashboard/project/_/settings/infrastructure) to accommodate for short-term disk stress. 109 110 115

2	id: 'ai-ivf-indexes'
3	title: 'IVFFlat indexes'
4	description: 'Understanding IVFFlat indexes in pgvector'
5	sidebar_label: 'IVFFlat indexes'
6	---
7	
8	IVFFlat is a type of vector index for approximate nearest neighbor search. It is a frequently used index type that can improve performance when querying highly-dimensional vectors, like those representing embeddings.
9	
10	## Choosing an index
11	
12	Today `pgvector` supports two types of indexes:
13	
14	- [HNSW](/docs/guides/ai/vector-indexes/hnsw-indexes)
15	- [IVFFlat](/docs/guides/ai/vector-indexes/ivf-indexes)
16	
17	In general we recommend using [HNSW](/docs/guides/ai/vector-indexes/hnsw-indexes) because of its [performance](/blog/increase-performance-pgvector-hnsw#hnsw-performance-1536-dimensions) and [robustness against changing data](/docs/guides/ai/vector-indexes/hnsw-indexes#when-should-you-create-hnsw-indexes). If you have a special use case that requires IVFFlat instead, keep reading.
18	
19	## Usage
20	
21	The way you create an IVFFlat index depends on the distance operator you are using. `pgvector` includes 3 distance operators:
22	
23	| Operator | Description            | [**Operator class**](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createopclass.html) |
24	| -------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
25	| `<->`    | Euclidean distance     | `vector_l2_ops`                                                                      |
26	| `<#>`    | negative inner product | `vector_ip_ops`                                                                      |
27	| `<=>`    | cosine distance        | `vector_cosine_ops`                                                                  |
28	
29	Use the following SQL commands to create an IVFFlat index for the operator(s) used in your queries.
30	
31	### Euclidean L2 distance (`vector_l2_ops`)
32	
33	```sql
34	create index on items using ivfflat (column_name vector_l2_ops) with (lists = 100);
35	```
36	
37	### Inner product (`vector_ip_ops`)
38	
39	```sql
40	create index on items using ivfflat (column_name vector_ip_ops) with (lists = 100);
41	```
42	
43	### Cosine distance (`vector_cosine_ops`)
44	
45	```sql
46	create index on items using ivfflat (column_name vector_cosine_ops) with (lists = 100);
47	```
48	
49	Currently vectors with up to 2,000 dimensions can be indexed.
50	
51	## How does IVFFlat work?
52	
53	IVF stands for 'inverted file indexes'. It works by clustering your vectors in order to reduce the similarity search scope. Rather than comparing a vector to every other vector, the vector is only compared against vectors within the same cell cluster (or nearby clusters, depending on your configuration).
54	
55	### Inverted lists (cell clusters)
56	
57	When you create the index, you choose the number of inverted lists (cell clusters). Increase this number to speed up queries, but at the expense of recall.
58	
59	For example, to create an index with 100 lists on a column that uses the cosine operator:
60	
61	```sql
62	create index on items using ivfflat (column_name vector_cosine_ops) with (lists = 100);
63	```
64	
65	For more info on the different operators, see [Distance operations](#distance-operators).
66	
67	For every query, you can set the number of probes (1 by default). The number of probes corresponds to the number of nearby cells to probe for a match. Increase this for better recall at the expense of speed.
68	
69	To set the number of probes for the duration of the session run:
70	
71	```sql
72	set ivfflat.probes = 10;
73	```
74	
75	To set the number of probes only for the current transaction run:
76	
77	```sql
78	begin;
79	set local ivfflat.probes = 10;
80	select ...
81	commit;
82	```
83	
84	If the number of probes is the same as the number of lists, exact nearest neighbor search will be performed and the planner won't use the index.
85	
86	### Approximate nearest neighbor
87	
88	One important note with IVF indexes is that nearest neighbor search is approximate, since exact search on high dimensional data can't be indexed efficiently. This means that similarity results will change (slightly) after you add an index (trading recall for speed).
89	
90	## When should you create IVFFlat indexes?
91	
92	`pgvector` recommends building IVFFlat indexes only after the table has sufficient data, so that the internal IVFFlat cell clusters are based on your data's distribution. Anytime the distribution changes significantly, consider rebuilding indexes.
93	
94	## Resources
95	
96	Read more about indexing on `pgvector`'s [GitHub page](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector#indexing).

---
id: 'ai-ivf-indexes'
title: 'IVFFlat indexes'
description: 'Understanding IVFFlat indexes in pgvector'
sidebar_label: 'IVFFlat indexes'
---

IVFFlat is a type of vector index for approximate nearest neighbor search. It is a frequently used index type that can improve performance when querying highly-dimensional vectors, like those representing embeddings.

## Choosing an index

Today `pgvector` supports two types of indexes:

- [HNSW](/docs/guides/ai/vector-indexes/hnsw-indexes)
- [IVFFlat](/docs/guides/ai/vector-indexes/ivf-indexes)

In general we recommend using [HNSW](/docs/guides/ai/vector-indexes/hnsw-indexes) because of its [performance](/blog/increase-performance-pgvector-hnsw#hnsw-performance-1536-dimensions) and [robustness against changing data](/docs/guides/ai/vector-indexes/hnsw-indexes#when-should-you-create-hnsw-indexes). If you have a special use case that requires IVFFlat instead, keep reading.

## Usage

The way you create an IVFFlat index depends on the distance operator you are using. `pgvector` includes 3 distance operators:

| Operator | Description            | [**Operator class**](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createopclass.html) |
| -------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `<->`    | Euclidean distance     | `vector_l2_ops`                                                                      |
| `<#>`    | negative inner product | `vector_ip_ops`                                                                      |
| `<=>`    | cosine distance        | `vector_cosine_ops`                                                                  |

Use the following SQL commands to create an IVFFlat index for the operator(s) used in your queries.

### Euclidean L2 distance (`vector_l2_ops`)

```sql
create index on items using ivfflat (column_name vector_l2_ops) with (lists = 100);
```

### Inner product (`vector_ip_ops`)

```sql
create index on items using ivfflat (column_name vector_ip_ops) with (lists = 100);
```

### Cosine distance (`vector_cosine_ops`)

```sql
create index on items using ivfflat (column_name vector_cosine_ops) with (lists = 100);
```

Currently vectors with up to 2,000 dimensions can be indexed.

## How does IVFFlat work?

IVF stands for 'inverted file indexes'. It works by clustering your vectors in order to reduce the similarity search scope. Rather than comparing a vector to every other vector, the vector is only compared against vectors within the same cell cluster (or nearby clusters, depending on your configuration).

### Inverted lists (cell clusters)

When you create the index, you choose the number of inverted lists (cell clusters). Increase this number to speed up queries, but at the expense of recall.

For example, to create an index with 100 lists on a column that uses the cosine operator:

```sql
create index on items using ivfflat (column_name vector_cosine_ops) with (lists = 100);
```

For more info on the different operators, see [Distance operations](#distance-operators).

For every query, you can set the number of probes (1 by default). The number of probes corresponds to the number of nearby cells to probe for a match. Increase this for better recall at the expense of speed.

To set the number of probes for the duration of the session run:

```sql
set ivfflat.probes = 10;
```

To set the number of probes only for the current transaction run:

```sql
begin;
set local ivfflat.probes = 10;
select ...
commit;
```

If the number of probes is the same as the number of lists, exact nearest neighbor search will be performed and the planner won't use the index.

### Approximate nearest neighbor

One important note with IVF indexes is that nearest neighbor search is approximate, since exact search on high dimensional data can't be indexed efficiently. This means that similarity results will change (slightly) after you add an index (trading recall for speed).

## When should you create IVFFlat indexes?

`pgvector` recommends building IVFFlat indexes only after the table has sufficient data, so that the internal IVFFlat cell clusters are based on your data's distribution. Anytime the distribution changes significantly, consider rebuilding indexes.

## Resources

Read more about indexing on `pgvector`'s [GitHub page](https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector#indexing).

content.text:
Root cause: your **IVFFlat** index built with `lists = 100` was sized for the original data distribution. IVFFlat clusters degrade in recall/speed as the table grows past what the index was tuned for — docs say to rebuild it after significant growth (`guides/ai/vector-indexes/ivf-indexes.mdx`, "When should you create IVFFlat indexes?"). At 250K+ rows, probes are scanning more of each cluster, causing the RPC to exceed your client's read timeout.

Recommended fix (per `troubleshooting/increase-vector-lookup-speeds-by-applying-an-hsnw-index-ohLHUM.mdx`): switch to an **HNSW** index instead, since Supabase docs explicitly recommend it over IVFFlat for performance and robustness against changing/growing data (`ivf-indexes.mdx` line 17):

```sql
drop index if exists <ivfflat_index_name>;
create index on public.first_table using hnsw (subtitle_embedding vector_cosine_ops);
```

Given you plan to grow to 650K+ rows, build it via an external `psql` connection with `maintenance_work_mem` raised and `statement_timeout = '0'`, since the Dashboard has a ~2 min query limit (same file, steps 2–5).
